# The Cost of Intelligence, Episode 19: A Kilo to Orbit Fell From $18,500 to $3,400


### Space Race Sunday checks the orbital pipeline, SpaceX’s chip loans grow to $44B, Texas permits 620 gas engines for one OpenAI campus, and one cache flip cut an AI bill 40%.


[Strong Compute](https://substack.com/@strongcompute)


Nov 23, 2026


*Listen to this episode on [Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/6i34Qxl6l98x6yzz4dGNf2) or watch it on [YouTube](https://youtu.be/5jLFd8nuPQE) .*


Welcome back to


**The Cost of Intelligence** , our comedy news show about the money behind AI. Each episode, Ben Sand reads the industry’s invoice and asks one question: are you getting more intelligence per dollar?


This week: our first


**Space Race Sunday** checks what’s actually working in orbit, and what a kilo to orbit costs now.


**SpaceX’s chip financing** priced at about $44 billion, and the lenders want the chips on the ground.


**Texas** permitted a 2.6 gigawatt gas plant for one OpenAI campus. On


**Ramp’s numbers** , a business AI token got 11% cheaper in four weeks, and businesses spent 12% more anyway. Plus three cuts from the Department of Token Efficiency. Here’s the written version, with every source linked.


---


## Space Race Sunday


Our bet here at TCI: one day, compute in orbit outgrows all the compute on Earth. So let’s check the pipeline. House rule: hardware in orbit counts. Renderings don’t.


**The scoreboard.**


-


**Starcloud** launched an


**Nvidia H100** into orbit last November, and ran models on it in December (


[Starcloud](https://www.starcloud.com/starcloud-1) ).


-


**Google’s Suncatcher** test satellite, built with Planet, launched October 1 (


[Google](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/google-research/project-suncatcher-prototype/) ). It carries


**four TPUs** and runs one at a time (


[TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/30/googles-first-data-center-satellite-is-online-and-writing-poetry/) ). On October 30 it answered its first prompt from orbit, with a haiku (


[Google](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/google-research/project-suncatcher-satellite-response/) ).


-


**China** has launched


**twenty computing satellites** in two batches, but hasn’t said what chips are inside (


[CGTN](https://news.cgtn.com/news/2026-10-14/China-launches-eight-satellites-for-space-based-computing-1ReYc4EvEQ0/p.html) ).


**The pipeline.**


-


**Starcloud-2** is a pair of


**8 kW** satellites on 2027 rideshares (


[TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/21/starcloud-raises-200-million-for-orbital-data-centers-as-launch-options-dry-up/) ). Starcloud’s CEO says the first one launches in January.


-


Starcloud has booked a whole


**Rocket Lab Neutron** rocket for


**2029** (


[NewSpace Economy, on Rocket Lab’s release](https://newspaceeconomy.ca/2026/11/10/rocket-lab-neutron-orders-515-million-launch-business/) ), and has asked the FCC to fly up to


**88,000** satellites (


[TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/21/starcloud-raises-200-million-for-orbital-data-centers-as-launch-options-dry-up/) ).


-


**Google’s** next step is twin interconnected satellites in


**2027** (


-


**SpaceX** says each planned AI satellite carries about


**175 kilowatts** of compute, close to one rack of Nvidia’s newest chips, with production as soon as late 2027 (


[SpaceX](https://www.spacex.com/spacexai/starmind) ;


[Interesting Engineering](https://interestingengineering.com/ai-robotics/spacex-nvidia-starmind-ai1-compute-payload) ). Some reports describe 175 kW as the maximum.


**And the ride keeps getting cheaper.** From 1970 to 2000, a kilo to orbit averaged about


**$18,500** (in 2018 dollars), a NASA study found (


[NASA](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20180007067/downloads/20180007067.pdf) ). At Falcon 9’s


**$74 million** list price, it’s roughly


**$3,400** a kilo today (our arithmetic, at 22,000 kg;


[SpaceX](https://www.spacex.com/media/Capabilities&Services.pdf) ). Google’s Suncatcher paper projects


**$200 or less** by the mid-2030s (


[arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19468) ), and Elon Musk says Starship gets it


**under $100** (


[Off Planet News](https://offplanetnews.com/2026/11/09/musk-expects-starship-to-cut-cost-of-cargo-to-orbit-below/) ).


A rendering has never once needed a radiator.


*Per-dollar verdict: today, a handful of chips work in orbit. The pipeline holds tens of thousands of satellites, and the ride keeps getting cheaper. Our bet: the biggest computer ever built won’t be on Earth.*


---


## SpaceX’s chip loans


On Friday, SpaceX’s GPU financing priced at about


**$44 billion** , Apollo and Goldman Sachs said, oversubscribed and upsized on investor demand (


[Apollo](https://ir.apollo.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/662/apollo-and-goldman-sachs-announce-pricing-of-44-billion) ). That’s up from the roughly


**$40 billion** SpaceX disclosed in October (


[TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/26/spacex-locks-in-40b-gpu-financing-deal-with-apollo/) ).


The FT reports the lenders asked that none of the chips go into SpaceX’s orbital data centers (


[TechCrunch, citing the FT](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/chips-can-survive-the-space-environment-can-their-financing/) ). Apollo’s release says the chips are for SpaceX’s terrestrial compute buildout anyway.


Our take: a media storm in a teacup. The lenders wanted different terms, and the money showed up. Borrowing against GPUs is normal for the big compute landlords.


*Per-dollar verdict: different terms, same chips. More GPUs on the ground means more GPU hours for sale.*


---


## Power on the ground


Texas regulators issued


**VoltaGrid** an air permit for a gas plant of about


**2.6 gigawatts** , with


**620** gas engines. It feeds


**Stargate Frontier** , the campus Vantage is building for OpenAI (


[Cleanview](https://cleanview.co/reports/behind-the-meter-data-centers/full-report/stargate-frontier) ). Per the script’s read of the permit, it replaces a permit for about 700 megawatts, so the plant got more than three and a half times bigger.


That’s the power of nearly


**15,000** of those SpaceX satellites (our arithmetic, at 175 kW each). In one permit.


*Per-dollar verdict: more power on the ground means more tokens for sale. But the gas bill rides along with every one of them.*


---


## The price of a business AI token


**Ramp** sells corporate cards and AI spend software, and tracks AI use at more than


**85,000** US businesses. Its token figures come from its own AI spend customers (


[Ramp AI Index](https://ramp.com/data/ai-index) ). In the week to November 15:


-


Ramp’s blend of OpenAI and Anthropic prices fell to


**45 cents per million tokens** , down


**11%** in four weeks.


-


Over the same four weeks, businesses used


**27%** more tokens, and spent


**12%** more.


-


Of every token dollar,


**Anthropic** took


**59 cents** ,


**OpenAI 37** , and xAI (now SpaceXSI)


**2** .


Buyers got more tokens for every dollar. Then they spent the savings on more tokens. Jevons is taking a victory lap.


*Per-dollar verdict: the token got cheaper, and the bill got bigger. Nobody has ever eaten just one.*


All that to drive a future filled with


**Sky-high Intelligence** , or SI for short. Literally, if SpaceX gets its way.


---


## Department of Token Efficiency


Chainsaw fueled. Spreadsheets open.


**Cut one: ArisGlobal cached the wrong half.** ArisGlobal makes drug-safety software. Its AI reads reports of bad reactions to medicines and pulls out about


**130** fields (


[AWS](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/how-arisglobal-scaled-generative-ai-inference-on-amazon-bedrock/) ). In six months, the shared part of its prompt grew about


**2.5x** , and the cost per case more than tripled.


It first cached each report, because it was the biggest part. That was the mistake: a report gets reused for one case, but the shared prompt gets reused by every case, for every customer. So they flipped it: shared prompt first, cached, report after. Now


**65%** of input tokens come from the cache, input costs fell by about


**half** , and the monthly AI bill fell about


**40%** , at more than


**19 billion** tokens a month.


Cache what everyone reuses, not what’s biggest.


**The fine print:** it’s an AWS blog post, written with ArisGlobal’s team. Percentages only, no dollar figures.


**Cut two: Popp stopped asking a genius for a yes or no.** Popp builds AI that screens job candidates over text and email. Every incoming message went to an OpenAI model, even a plain opt-out. Popp swapped those calls for small decision models called


**Jev** , from TypeSafe, which answer yes or no with a probability (


[Explosion](https://explosion.ai/blog/popp-llms-jev) ). Token costs fell about


**76%** , the typical check went from


**1.5 seconds to about 0.2** , and it got more accurate on every decision the post compares.


**The fine print:** it’s a case study on the blog of Explosion, which sells the tool Popp used to switch. Two checks now cost more than twice as much per call, and scoring résumés is still Popp’s biggest cost.


**Cut three: the Mac Studio rematch.** Exo Labs got Thinking Machines’ small open model


**Inkling 2 Mini** (


[Thinking Machines](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-mini/) ) running on one Mac Studio with Apple’s M5 Ultra, at


**210 tokens a second** (


[Exo Labs on X](https://x.com/exolabs/status/2123953913342935486) ). Exo says it built a weather app


**1.8x** as fast as Claude Sonnet 5.5. Hugging Face co-founder Julien Chaumond shared it as


**11x cheaper (API pricing)** , adding: “this is how local and open source AI is going to win” (


[Julien Chaumond on X](https://x.com/julien_c/status/2124099948937388225) ).


One catch on “cheaper”: the 11x compares Thinking Machines’ API price with Anthropic’s API price. It’s not what it costs to run the Mac on your desk.


**The fine print:** one app, in Exo’s own demo. Exo worked with Thinking Machines to get the model running, and Exo hasn’t published the math behind 11x.


The Department of Token Efficiency. Read the meter, not the brochure.
